title: CV
Puqiu Zhao, PhD student
text:
I am a 2nd year PhD student in the Department of Political Economy since October 2025, fully funded by the London Interdisciplinary Social Science Doctoral Training Partnership and UKRI Economic and Social Research Council.
My main research agenda centres on climate politics and voting behaviour, with a regional focus on European countries. In particular, I study how stringent climate and energy policies influence potential Green backlash under exogenous shocks.
My broader research interests include the mechanism of shifting positions of far-right populist parties regarding climate change and the energy transition, and other important issues in environmental and climate politics, such as climate activism, climate denialism, microplastic governance and international climate change negotiations.

title: Puqiu Zhao, PhD student
text:
Work in progress

  The Ebb after the Wave: Explaining the Diverging Electoral Fortunes of European Green Parties after 2019
  Puqiu Zhao · Work in progress · 2026
  Green Parties · Electoral Politics · Crisis
  However, we still do not know why some Green parties have declined while others have gained ground.
  
    Project page
    Literature
    
      Read abstract
      European Green parties’ electoral performance provides an important barometer of public attitudes towards climate change and societal demand for further climate action. European Parliament elections are particularly valuable because, as second-order elections, they allow voters to express their preferences more sincerely. The 2019 election marked a significant breakthrough for Green parties, widely associated with the European Green Deal. However, most Green parties experienced declining vote shares in 2024.
      Existing studies explain the universal decline from the environmental and economic trade-off from the demand and spatial and issue competition from the supply. However, we still do not know why some Green parties have declined while others have gained ground. The paper offers a parsimonious theoretical explanation based on the sanctioning and selection logic, and explains the variation through three main mechanisms: strategic policy changes by Green parties, heterogeneous external shocks, and signals sent by competing political parties. We empirically examine these mechanisms and primarily find that heterogeneous external shocks alone cannot account for the divergence. The paper identifies the party characteristics that enable Green parties to sustain electoral support during the economic crisis.

title: The Ebb after the Wave: Explaining the Diverging Electoral Fortunes of European Green Parties after 2019
text:
About the project
European Green parties’ electoral performance provides an important barometer of public attitudes towards climate change and societal demand for further climate action. European Parliament elections are particularly valuable because, as second-order elections, they allow voters to express their preferences more sincerely. The 2019 election marked a significant breakthrough for Green parties, widely associated with the European Green Deal. However, most Green parties experienced declining vote shares in 2024.
Existing studies explain the universal decline from the environmental and economic trade-off from the demand and spatial and issue competition from the supply. However, we still do not know why some Green parties have declined while others have gained ground. The paper offers a parsimonious theoretical explanation based on the sanctioning and selection logic, and explains the variation through three main mechanisms: strategic policy changes by Green parties, heterogeneous external shocks, and signals sent by competing political parties. We empirically examine these mechanisms and primarily find that heterogeneous external shocks alone cannot account for the divergence. The paper identifies the party characteristics that enable Green parties to sustain electoral support during the economic crisis.
